questions.q: Explain why computers represent all data in binary.

markPoints.concept: the components in a computer have two states, such as on and off
accept: on and off|on or off|high and low|current|voltage|switch
markPoints.exemplar: The circuits inside a computer can only be on or off.

markPoints.concept: so a 1 and a 0 can represent those two states directly
markPoints.exemplar: So a 1 can mean on and a 0 can mean off.

questions.example: The circuits inside a computer can only be in one of two states, on or off, so a 1 and a 0 map straight onto those two states and everything has to be built out of them.
questions.paraphrase: Hardware only has two conditions, current flowing or not, which means a one and a zero represent them exactly.
questions.feedback: Two states in the hardware, two digits in the number system.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 6 — Units lab, station 1: Why binary?

questions.q: How many different values can be represented by one bit?
questions.feedback: One bit is one binary digit: 0 or 1.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 6 — Units lab, station 1: Why binary?

questions.q: Match each unit to how many bits it contains.
questions.feedback: A nibble is half a byte, which is where its name comes from.

questions.q: A file is 2 KB. How many bytes is that?
questions.feedback: This course uses 1 kB = 1,000 bytes, which is the convention OCR uses.
questions.hint: How many bytes does this course take a kilobyte to be?

questions.q: A memory card holds 64 GB. How many megabytes is that?
questions.feedback: One gigabyte is 1,000 megabytes, so 64 GB = 64,000 MB.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 6 — Units lab, station 4: Converting units

questions.q: A video is 4.5 GB. How many kilobytes is that?
questions.feedback: GB to MB to kB is two steps of a thousand: 4.5 × 1,000 × 1,000.
questions.hint: Go one unit at a time rather than trying to do it in one jump.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 6 — Units lab, station 4: Converting units

questions.q: A hard disk holds 3 TB. How many gigabytes is that?
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 6 — Units lab, station 4: Converting units

questions.q: Put these units in order, smallest first.
questions.feedback: A nibble is four bits, a byte is eight, and from there it is steps of a thousand all the way up.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 6 — Units lab, station 4: Converting units

questions.q: Which unit comes immediately after a terabyte?
questions.feedback: Kilo, mega, giga, tera, peta — each a thousand times the one before.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 6 — Units lab, station 4: Converting units

questions.q: A school has 1,500 photographs, each 4 MB. How many gigabytes of storage are needed?

methodMark.label: works out the total in megabytes (6,000 MB)

questions.feedback: 1,500 × 4 = 6,000 MB, and 6,000 ÷ 1,000 = 6 GB. The method mark is for reaching 6,000 MB even if the last step goes wrong.
